source.title: CBSE Sample Question Paper, Class X (2025-26), Social Science (087)
source.subject: social-science
source.notes: This is the CBSE Sample Question Paper for the 2025-26 academic session, published on the CBSE Academic site's SQP_CLASSX_2025-26 listing page. It is published for the 2025-26 session board exam, so examYear is set to 2026 (the exam year the SQP prepares students for), matching the convention used for other CBSE SQPs in this project. Paper prints 'SOCIAL SCIENCE-Code- 087', 12 printed pages, 38 questions across four 20-mark sections (A-History, B-Geography, C-Political Science, D-Economics), Maximum Marks 80, Time Allowed 3 hours. No paper code, set code or series code is printed (this is a sample paper, not a numbered live question paper). Three 'Note: The following question is for Visually Impaired Candidates only in lieu of Q. No. X' alternative questions are printed (in lieu of Q.2, Q.19 and Q.21); these VI-only alternatives are not imported as separate questions, per project convention. Q.9 (2 marks) asks students to identify two places marked on an outline map of India from descriptive clues and write their names; the map itself (printed on page 12) is not reproduced, but the question text stands alone (the clues identify the places without needing to see the map), so it is imported with hasFigure true and the map flagged as not reproduced. Q.19 (3 marks) asks students to 'locate and label' features directly on the outline map 'with suitable symbols' — this is a pure map-marking task with no textual answer to record, so it is NOT imported (its VI-only textual alternative is also skipped, consistent with the VI-alternative rule above). The blank outline map itself (page 12, shared by Q.9 and Q.19) is not reproduced. The marking scheme (SocialScience-MS.pdf) has several places where the PDF's column/margin layout interleaves unrelated text; these are flagged per-question where they affect an official answer.
source.usage: Official CBSE publication, freely available on cbseacademic.nic.in; question text reproduced for study with attribution and a link to the original. Figures are not reproduced.

questions.text: Thousands of people fled Europe for America in the 19th century due to -
options: Widespread poverty and deadly diseases
Frequent famines and poor living conditions
Continuous wars and political instability
Harsh climate and repeated natural disasters

officialAnswer.text: (A) / Widespread poverty and deadly diseases

questions.text: Louise-Sebastien Mercier proclaimed “Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world! Tremble before the virtual writer!” Who are referred to as the tyrants in this context?
options: Educated classes who wanted to change the society
Absolutist institutions like monarchy and church
Authors of the new books
Printing press

officialAnswer.text: (B) / Absolutist institutions like monarchy and church

questions.text: “The Silk route was a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world.” Explain the statement with any two examples.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Chinese pottery, textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia also travelled the same route. In return, precious metals - gold and silver - flowed from Europe to Asia.
2. Trade and cultural exchange went hand in hand. Buddhism from India spread in several directions through intersecting points on the silk routes.
3. Early Christian missionaries travelled this route to reach Asia and Muslim preachers took the same route a few centuries later. (Any 2 points)

questions.text: ‘Sometimes the new crops could make the difference between life and death.’. Explain the statement with any two examples.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Sometimes new crops like potatoes could make the difference between life and death. It was with the introduction of the humble potato that Europe's poor began to eat well, eat better and live longer.
2. Ireland's poor peasants became so dependent on potatoes that when the potato crop was destroyed by disease in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands of peasants died of starvation.

questions.text: ‘A variety of cultural processes played an important role in developing a sense of nationalism in India’. Support the statement with suitable examples.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists five value points and accepts any three; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Figure or Image - The identity of India came to be visually associated with the image of Bharat Mata. This image was created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. Rabindranath Tagore painted his famous image of Bharat Mata; she is portrayed as an ascetic figure - calm, composed, divine and spiritual.
2. Songs - Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland; it was included in his novel Anandmath and widely sung during the Swadeshi Movement in Bengal.
3. Folklore - Indian folklore was revived; nationalists began recording folk tales sung by bards, and in Bengal Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths, while in Madras Natesa Sastri published a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales.
4. Flag - a Swadeshi tricolour (red, green and yellow) with eight lotuses and a crescent moon was designed in Bengal; by 1921 Gandhiji had designed the Swaraj flag (red, green and white) with a spinning wheel.
5. Re-interpretation of History - Indians began looking into the past to discover India's great achievements in art, architecture, science, religion, law and philosophy. (Any three points to be considered)

questions.text: Salt March 'became an effective tool of resistance against colonialism.’ Analyse the statement with suitable reasons.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Salt became an effective tool of resistance against colonialism because Gandhiji found in salt a powerful bond that would unite the nation, as it was consumed by all, rich and poor alike.
2. Gandhiji's letter to Viceroy Irwin stated eleven demands; the most stirring was to abolish the salt tax imposed by the colonial government.
3. Irwin's unwillingness to negotiate forced Gandhiji to start his Salt March, which was joined by thousands and developed the feeling of nationalism.
4. People in different parts of the country broke the salt law and manufactured salt, demonstrating in front of government salt factories.
5. People unitedly followed Gandhiji's call - they refused to pay taxes and revenues, picketed liquor shops, boycotted foreign clothes, resigned from government jobs and violated forest laws. (Any three points to be considered)

questions.text: ‘In Britain the formation of the nation-state was not the result of a sudden upheaval or revolution but was the result of a long-drawn-out process.’ Analyse this statement with suitable reasons.

officialAnswer.text:
1. In Britain the formation of the nation-state was not the result of a sudden upheaval or revolution. The primary identities of the people who inhabited the British Isles were ethnic ones - such as English, Welsh, Scot or Irish.
2. The Act of Union (1707) between England and Scotland resulted in the formation of the 'United Kingdom of Great Britain', which meant England was able to impose its influence on Scotland; Scotland's distinctive culture and political institutions were systematically suppressed.
3. The Scottish Highlanders were forbidden to speak their Gaelic language or wear their national dress, and large numbers were forcibly driven out of their homeland.
4. The English helped the Protestants of Ireland establish dominance over a largely Catholic country. Catholic revolts against British dominance were suppressed; Ireland was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom in 1801.
5. The symbols of the new Britain - the British flag, the national anthem, the English language - were actively promoted, and the older nations survived only as subordinate partners in this union.

questions.text: ‘The Treaty of Vienna was drawn up in 1815 with the object of undoing most of the changes that had come about in Europe during the Napoleonic wars.’ Highlight the significant provisions of this treaty.

officialAnswer.text:
1. The Bourbon dynasty, which had been deposed during the French Revolution, was restored to power, and France lost the territories it had annexed under Napoleon.
2. A series of states were set up on the boundaries of France to prevent future French expansion - the kingdom of the Netherlands (including Belgium) was set up in the north, and Genoa was added to Piedmont in the south.
3. Prussia was given important new territories on its western frontiers, while Austria was given control of northern Italy.
4. The German confederation of 39 states set up by Napoleon was left untouched. In the east, Russia was given part of Poland while Prussia was given a portion of Saxony.
5. The main intention was to restore the monarchies that had been overthrown by Napoleon, and create a new conservative order in Europe.

questions.text:
Read the given text and answer the following questions:
Why Newspapers?
Krishnaji Trimbuck Ranade inhabitant of Poona intends to publish a Newspaper in the Marathi Language with a view of affording useful information on every topic of local interest. It will be open for free discussion on subjects of general utility, scientific investigation and the speculations connected with the antiquities, statistics, curiosities, history and geography of the country and of the Deccan especially... the patronage and support of all interested in the diffusion of knowledge and Welfare of the People is earnestly solicited.
Bombay Telegraph and Courier, 6 January 1849
“The task of the native newspapers and political associations is identical to the role of the Opposition in the House of Commons in Parliament in England. That is to critically examine government policy to suggest improvements, by removing those parts that will not be to the benefit of the people, and also by ensuring speedy implementation.
These associations ought to carefully study the particular issues, gather diverse relevant information on the nation as well as on what are the possible and desirable improvements, and this will surely earn it considerable influence”.
Source: Native Opinion, 3 April 1870
8.1. Explain the main reason for publishing newspapers by Krishnaji. (1)
8.2. How was the task of native newspaper and political association seen identical to the role of the opposition? (1)
8.3. Analyze the reasons for the popularity of newspapers during the 19th century. (2)
extractionIssues: Sub-part marks shown in brackets were printed in the margin.

officialAnswer.text:
8.1 Krishnaji wanted to publish significant information about societal developments in the areas of politics, science, and other fields in order to inform the public.
8.2 The media used to criticise and analyse government policies were local newspapers and political organisations. As a result, both of these served as the government's opposition.
8.3 Reasons for popularity of newspapers during the 19th century are:
i. The political developments in the country began to interest a sizable portion of society, and this information was skillfully presented in the newspapers.
ii. Newspapers started to serve as a source for societal advancements in social, cultural, and scientific...

options: These places mostly have forests managed as reserved or protected forests for conservation.
They rely on unclassed forests and local community management for forest conservation.
They have forest resources and primarily focus on industrial development.

options: Haryana
Punjab

questions.text: Which of the following statements best evaluates the overall goal of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchaee Yojana?
options: Addressing the negative ecological effects of large dams by reducing water usage.
To provide better irrigation systems and sustainable water conservation practices for farmers.
Shifting farmers from traditional crops to more commercial, water-intensive crops.
Preserve the natural river flow and prevent the fragmentation of aquatic ecosystems.

officialAnswer.text: B - To provide better irrigation systems and sustainable water conservation practices for farmers.

questions.text: Rice is grown as a commercial crop in Haryana and Punjab, but as a subsistence crop in Odisha. Using your understanding of geographical factors and economic practices, explain why rice cultivation differs in these regions.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists several points under three headings (climate/irrigation, market access, farming practices); trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
Climate and Irrigation: Haryana and Punjab have a well-developed irrigation system (e.g. canal irrigation from the Sutlej-Yamuna Link Canal), which allows large-scale commercial cultivation of rice; in contrast, Odisha has a more monsoonal climate and rice farming is often rainfed and mainly for local consumption.
Economic Factors (Market Access): In Punjab and Haryana, rice is grown for commercial purposes to meet national and international demand, with proximity to markets, government procurement systems and transport networks enabling export of surplus rice; in Odisha, rice is mostly grown for personal or local use, making it a subsistence crop.
Farming Practices: Punjab and Haryana use modern farming techniques, machinery and high-yielding varieties; Odisha's rice farming is more traditional and focused on family sustenance. (Or any other relevant point(s); any 2 points, at least one related to climate and one economic)

questions.text: Person P is willing to establish a mineral based industry. He has been advised to set up a bauxite industry in Odisha as a suitable way to make a profitable venture. Analyse the possible reasons behind the advice given to her.
extractionIssues: Official answer points 2-5 are fragmentary/run together in the marking scheme PDF (e.g. point 2 trails off at 'such as iron,'); lightly joined here into complete sentences - check against the PDF.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Odisha was the largest bauxite-producing state in India in 2016-17. Panchpatmali deposits in Koraput district are the most important bauxite deposits in the state.
2. Aluminium is an important metal because it combines the strength of metals such as iron with extreme lightness.
3. It is a good alternative to other metals due to its extreme lightness.
4. It also has good conductivity.
5. It has great malleability. (any other relevant point - 5 points)

questions.text: ‘Coal is the most important and abundant fossil fuel in India.’ Justify the statement by evaluating the significant role it plays in the growth of the Indian economy in its different forms.

officialAnswer.text:
Significance: coal is used for power generation, to supply energy to industry as well as for domestic needs; India is highly dependent on coal for meeting its commercial energy requirements, e.g. in metallurgy (any other relevant point; at least 2).
Variety of coal types (by degree of compression, depth and time of burial):
1. Peat - decaying plants in swamps produce peat, which has low carbon and high moisture content and low heating capacity.
2. Lignite - a low-grade brown coal, soft with high moisture content; principal reserves are in Neyveli, Tamil Nadu, used for generation of electricity.
3. Bituminous coal - coal buried deep and subjected to increased temperatures; the most popular coal in commercial use; metallurgical coal is high-grade bituminous coal with special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces.
4. Anthracite - the highest quality hard coal.

questions.text:
Read the given text and answer the following questions:
Global pollution is rising due to rapid economic growth, population increases, and insufficient environmental management. This poses serious health risks for people and ecosystems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Contributing to these challenges, the global economy relies on deeply intertwined supply chains, sustained by more than 100 billion tons of raw materials entering the system each year. Intensive material consumption depletes natural resources and causes negative environmental impacts at every stage of the product lifecycle. Global waste is expected to increase to 3.4 billion tons by 2050.
Pollution of all types hinders development outcomes. Exposure to air pollution, water pollution, and hazardous chemicals and wastes like mercury, lead and persistent organic pollutants (POPs) causes debilitating and fatal illnesses, creates harmful living conditions, and destroys ecosystems. Pollution undermines sustainable economic growth, exacerbates poverty and inequality in both urban and rural areas, and significantly contributes to climate change. Poor people, who cannot afford to protect themselves from the negative impacts of pollution, end up suffering the most.
Pollution is the largest environmental cause of disease and premature death. It is estimated to be several times more deaths than from AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria combined. Global health crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, are reminders of the strong linkages between environment and health and of the need to address such linkages systematically.
[Source: https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/pollution]
18.1 Why do you think is global waste expected to increase by 2050? (1)
18.2 How do manufacturing industries cause pollution of different types? Explain with examples. (2)
18.3 Is it correct to consider pollution as a possible cause for worsening of the current global trends of poverty and inequality? Justify. (1)
extractionIssues: Sub-part marks shown in brackets were printed in the margin; official answer for 18.2 lists six points and is trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
18.1 Due to intensive material production and consumption.
18.2 Manufacturing industries are a major cause of: (1) air pollution - smoke from chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants, and burning of fossil fuels; (2) water pollution - organic and inorganic industrial wastes and effluents (from paper, pulp, chemical, textile, dyeing, petroleum, tannery and electroplating industries) discharged into rivers; (3) thermal pollution of water from hot water drained into rivers and ponds before cooling; (4) soil pollution from dumping of glass, chemicals, effluents and garbage; (5) groundwater contamination as rainwater percolates pollutants into the soil; (6) noise pollution from industrial and construction machinery. (Any two points)
18.3 Poor people cannot afford to protect themselves from the negative impacts of pollution and end up suffering the most; this also leads to social disparity/inequality due to the ill effects of poverty. (Can be explained with the help of an example)

questions.text:
Two statements are given as Assertion (A) and Reason(R). Study the statements carefully and identify the correct alternative:
Assertion (A): Exclusive attention to caste can produce negative results in democracy.
Reason (R): It can divert attention from other important issues thus leading to tensions, conflicts and even violence.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true

officialAnswer.text: A - Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.text: Highlight any two key features of federalism.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists seven value points and accepts any two; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
1. There are two or more levels (or tiers) of government.
2. Different tiers of government govern the same citizens, but each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration.
3. The jurisdictions of the respective levels or tiers of government are specified in the constitution, so the existence and authority of each tier of government is constitutionally guaranteed.
4. The fundamental provisions of the constitution cannot be unilaterally changed by one level of government; such changes require the consent of both levels of government.
5. Courts have the power to interpret the constitution and the powers of different levels of government, acting as an umpire if disputes arise. (Any two points to be considered)

questions.text: ‘Women in India face discrimination, disadvantages and oppression in many ways.’ Highlight any two aspects of life where you witness this inequality.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists five value points and accepts any two; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Education - literacy rate among women is only 54% compared with 76% among men; parents prefer to spend resources on sons' education rather than daughters'.
2. Low proportion of women in highly paid and valued jobs - even if a woman works more hours than a man, her work is not given the same importance, resulting in low-paid, low-valued jobs for women.
3. Women are paid less than men - despite the Equal Wages Act, women are paid less even for exactly the same work.
4. Preference for sons - in many parts of India parents prefer sons and find ways to abort the girl child, leading to a declining child sex ratio (927).
5. Exploitation at the workplace and domestic violence. (Any 2 points to be considered)

questions.text: ‘Democracy leads to peaceful and harmonious life among citizens in every sphere.’ Support this statement with suitable arguments.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists five value points and accepts any three; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Democracies accommodate various social divisions - for example, Belgium has peacefully solved her ethnic problems.
2. All democracies usually develop a procedure to conduct competition (elections, power-sharing etc.), reducing the possibility of tensions due to social divisions turning violent.
3. Democracy teaches people to respect differences and resolve conflicts peacefully; non-democratic countries either turn a blind eye to or suppress internal differences (e.g. Sri Lanka).
4. A democracy is not just rule by majority opinion - the majority always needs to work with the minority.
5. A democratic government ensures that majority rule does not become autocratic on the basis of religion, race or language. (Any three points to be considered)

questions.text: ‘Political parties play a significant role in the effective working of a democracy.’ Explain.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists six value points and asks for any five; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Parties contest elections - elections are fought mainly among candidates put up by political parties; in India, top party leaders choose candidates for contesting elections.
2. Parties put forward different policies and programmes, grouping together similar opinions to provide a direction for government policies.
3. Parties make laws for a country - laws are debated and passed in the legislature.
4. Parties that lose elections play the role of the opposition, voicing their views by criticizing the government for its failures or wrong policies.
5. Parties shape public opinion - they raise and highlight issues; many pressure groups are extensions of political parties.
6. Parties provide people access to government machinery and welfare schemes - it is easier for an ordinary citizen to approach a local party leader than a government officer. (Any 5 points)

questions.text: Analyse how the issue of leadership succession poses a challenge to political parties in India.

officialAnswer.text:
1. Most political parties do not practice open and transparent procedures for their functioning, so there are very few ways for an ordinary worker to rise to the top in a party.
2. Those who happen to be leaders are in a position of unfair advantage, as they favour people close to them or even their family members.
3. In many parties in India we see a trend of dynastic succession - top positions are always controlled by members of a particular family, which is unfair to other members of the party and bad for democracy.
4. This is so because people who do not have adequate experience or popular support come to occupy positions of power.
5. More than loyalty to party principles and policies, personal loyalty to the leader becomes more important - a tendency seen all over the world, even in older democracies.

questions.text:
Read the given text and answer the following questions:
Sri Lanka emerged as an independent country in 1948. The leaders of the Sinhala community sought to secure dominance over government by virtue of their majority. As a result, the democratically elected government adopted a series of MAJORITARIAN measures to establish Sinhala supremacy. Over the years, it created feelings of alienation among the Sri Lankan Tamils. They felt that none of the major political parties led by the Buddhist Sinhala leaders was sensitive to their language and culture. As a result, the relations between the Sinhala and Tamil communities strained over time. On the other hand, the Belgian leaders took a different path. They recognised the existence of regional differences and cultural diversities. Between 1970 and 1993, they amended their constitution four times to work out an arrangement that would enable everyone to live together within the same country.
Source-Adapted from Power Sharing, NCERT
28.1 State any two demands of Tamils in Sri Lanka. (1)
28.2 State the results of the Majoritarian Government in Sri Lanka. (1)
28.3 Explain any two provisions of the Belgian model of power sharing. (2)
extractionIssues: Sub-part marks shown in brackets were printed in the margin.

Official answer for 28.3 point 1 has overlapping columns in the marking-scheme PDF layout ('French / Any two / make decisions' interleaves with the sentence); reconstructed here as 'Dutch- and French-speaking ministers ... no single community can unilaterally make decisions' - check against the PDF.

officialAnswer.text:
28.1 (Any one) To recognise Tamil as an official language / Regional autonomy / Equality of opportunities in securing education and jobs.
28.2 The Majoritarian Government in Sri Lanka created distrust between Tamils and Sinhalas which resulted in civil war; thousands of people of both communities were killed and many families were forced to leave the country as refugees.
28.3 (Any two) 1. The Constitution prescribed that the number of Dutch- and French-speaking ministers shall be equal in the central government; some special laws require the support of a majority of members from each linguistic group, so no single community can unilaterally make decisions.
2. Many powers of the central government have been given to the state governments of the two regions; the state governments are not subordinate to the Central Government.
3. Brussels has a separate government in which Dutch and French have equal representation.
4. A third kind of 'community government' is elected by people belonging to one language community - Dutch, French or German-speaking - no matter where they live, with power over cultural, educational and language-related issues.

questions.text: Underemployment is caused when -
options: More workers are employed than actually required
Fewer workers are employed than actually required
Workers are paid more than their actual output
Jobs are given only to highly educated workers

officialAnswer.text: A - More workers are employed than actually required

questions.text: What can be inferred about the limitations of using per capita income (average income) to compare well-being across countries? Choose the correct option as the answer.
options: It shows how equally or unequally income is distributed among the people in a country.
The only measure needed to understand a country’s development is Per capita income.
It gives a basic idea of economic well-being but hides the income inequality.
It only reflects the industrial growth of a country and does not consider other important factors.

officialAnswer.text: C - It gives a basic idea of economic well-being but hides the income inequality, cost of living, or access to essential services.

questions.text: Which of the following examples best demonstrates how the tertiary sector supports both the primary and secondary sectors?
options: Farmers grow vegetables and sell them directly to consumers, with no transportation or storage involved.

A bakery bakes bread and uses delivery services to send the bread to local shops for sale, without any direct involvement of raw materials.
A company produces furniture from wood, but does not require any transport or retail services to sell the product.

officialAnswer.text: B - A factory makes shoes and uses raw materials like leather to create the product, relying on transport and retail stores to distribute the shoes.

options: Finance Ministry.
Reserve Bank of India.
State Bank of India.

questions.text: Person Z tries to explain how the requirement of a double coincidence of wants in a barter system limits trade and exchange. Which of the following justification do you think will be used by him/her?
options: It makes trade more complicated, as each person must have what the other person wants, limiting the pool of potential trade partners.
The barter system allows trade to be conducted more efficiently since both parties already know what they need from the transaction.
It increases the number of exchanges because each person can trade for exactly what they want.
The system creates value for goods by ensuring that both parties have a direct need for each other’s goods.

officialAnswer.text: A - It makes trade more complicated, as each person must have what the other person wants, limiting the pool of potential trade partners.

questions.text: Evaluate the utility of public services in contributing to the overall well-being of individuals and society.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme covers four headings (healthcare, education, sanitation, infrastructure) and asks for any two; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
Healthcare and Public Health: accessible and quality public healthcare is fundamental for maintaining a productive and healthy population; it reduces mortality rates and allows individuals to contribute meaningfully to the economy.
Education and Skill Development: public education systems provide equal learning opportunities to all citizens regardless of socioeconomic status, leading to increased literacy, skill development and innovation.
Sanitation and Clean Water: proper sanitation and clean water are vital for maintaining public health and preventing diseases such as cholera and dysentery, improving life expectancy and productivity.
Infrastructure Development: public infrastructure (roads, transport, energy) supports markets, businesses and industries and improves quality of life. (Or any other relevant point(s); any two)

questions.text: ‘Expanding access to loans in the formal sector is important, yet it is equally critical that these loans are accessible to all people for national development.’ Justify the statement.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists several bullet points and asks for any three; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
- Higher cost of borrowing from informal sources means a larger part of the earnings of the borrowers is used to repay the loan, leaving less income for themselves.
- In certain cases the high interest rate for borrowing can mean the amount to be repaid is greater than the income of the borrower, leading to increasing debt and a debt trap.
- People who might wish to start an enterprise by borrowing may not do so because of the high cost of borrowing.
- For these reasons, banks and cooperative societies need to lend more; this would lead to higher incomes and let more people borrow cheaply for a variety of needs, to grow crops, do business or set up small-scale industries. Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development. (Or any other relevant point(s); any 3)

questions.text: Highlight the significant three factors that have contributed to the growth of globalisation.

officialAnswer.text:
1. The movement of goods and services.
2. Information and communication technology.
3. Transportation technology.
4. Movement of people between countries.
5. Liberalisation of foreign trade and foreign investment policy. (Any other relevant point; any 3 well explained)

questions.text: A research student spoke with two people, M and N to learn about their work-related differences. On the basis of the interview conducted with both of them, the student concludes that while person M was working in an organized sector, person N was an employee of a workplace that was functioning in an unorganised way. Analyse the key differences between the two sectors that must have enabled the research student to come to this conclusion.
extractionIssues: Official answer scheme lists many bullet points for each sector; trimmed here to fit the length limit.

officialAnswer.text:
Working conditions of person M (organised sector): regular, assured employment with fixed terms; enterprises registered with the government and following legal rules (e.g. Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act); job security with clear working hours and benefits; overtime compensation; employee benefits like paid leave, provident fund, gratuity and medical benefits; safe working conditions; retirement/pension benefits; formal processes for employment.
Working conditions of person N (unorganised sector): irregular, low-paid jobs with no guarantee of continuous work; sector largely outside government control with few legal protections; no employee benefits (leave, overtime, medical); job insecurity, workers can be dismissed without notice; often seasonal work; many workers self-employed in small jobs like street vending or repair work; conditions influenced by the employer's whims; little enforcement of rules on working conditions.

questions.text: Privatisation can have both positive and negative effects on the economy. Support the statement with argument.

officialAnswer.text:
Positive effects: 1. Increased efficiency and productivity. 2. Improved quality of services. 3. Reduced government burden. 4. Any other relevant point(s).
Negative effects: 1. Exclusion of public welfare - profit being the only motive. 2. Loss of employment security. 3. Wide gap between rich and poor, due to inaccessibility of basic facilities. 4. Lower government accountability. 5. Any other relevant point(s). (Any 5 points to be accepted; at least 2 positive and 2 negative effects must be included)
